title: Area Between Two Curves
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Companion Doorway to Area Between Two Curves

This canonical is the **short-form doorway** to area between two curves: the top-minus-bottom integral, intersection finding, and the split protocol in one page. The parent canonical carries the full treatment; this companion mirrors the theorems, adds the deep readings, and drills four heavy-mark problems.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Basic formula:** area = ∫ₐᵇ[top − bottom]dx where top is the larger y on each strip — always nonnegative.
- **Intersections:** solve f(x) = g(x) to find a and b (and any interior crossings that force splits).
- **Split protocol:** if the curves cross inside [a, b], the top/bottom roles swap — partition at each crossing and sum the pieces.
- **With respect to y:** for horizontally simple regions, area = ∫[right − left]dy — choose the axis that minimises splits.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — Top Minus Bottom Is |Difference| Made Structured

- The area between curves is ∫|f − g|dx in principle; the **top-minus-bottom form is that absolute value resolved by knowledge of which curve is on top** — the intersection analysis converts |·| into an explicit order. Finding intersections is not bookkeeping; it is the absolute value's disassembly.
- **Interior crossings swap roles:** between two crossings the sandwich may flip — the strip picture (vertical slices, who is on top?) is the reliable test on each subinterval, and one test point per strip settles it.
- **Symmetric setups:** equal curves mirrored about an axis (y² = x vs x = 4-style pairs) often yield double-the-half regions — compute one symmetric half and double, provided the symmetry is verified, not assumed.

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Choosing the Slicing Axis

- **Vertical slices (dx)** suit curves given as y = f(x); **horizontal slices (dy)** suit curves given as x = g(y) or regions bounded left-right by functions of y. The choice that avoids splitting is the cheaper computation.
- **Parabola-and-line economy:** for y² = 4x and x = 1-style regions, integrating in dy uses one integral; in dx it needs two (the region's left boundary changes formula at the vertex). The slicing axis is a computational decision, made by counting the required splits.
- **Sanity checks:** the answer must be positive; a rough sketch bounds it (compare with an enclosing rectangle); a known special case (line under line = triangle) validates the setup.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — no interior crossing:** one integral, top minus bottom.
- **Type B — interior crossing:** split at the crossing, two integrals.
- **Type C — dy slicing:** horizontal strips for x = g(y) boundaries.
- **Type D — symmetric doubling:** verify symmetry, compute half, double.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Top minus bottom needs absolute values":** once the order is known per strip, plain subtraction is correct — the |·| was resolved by the analysis. **"Integrate in dx always":** count the splits; dy may halve the work.

**Area between curves — classified by the intersection pattern**

| Pattern | Set-up | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| One crossing pair | Integral (top - bottom) dx | Identify top on the whole interval |
| Curves cross inside | Split at every intersection | Top-bottom swaps sign at each crossing |
| Vertical simplicity | Integrate (right - left) dy | Cheaper when curves are x = g(y) |
| Enclosed region | Solve f = g for limits | Limits come from the curves, not the axis |
confusion: Integrating one curve and ignoring the other instead of taking the difference.
Using the same expression over the whole interval when the top curve changes partway.
Failing to find the intersection points, which is what actually bounds the region.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (6m): Find the area of the region bounded by y = x² and y = x.** — **Intersections:** x² = x ⟹ x = 0, 1 ⟹ limits [0, 1]. **Order test:** at x = 1/2: line 1/2 > parabola 1/4 ⟹ **line on top**. **Evaluate:** ∫₀¹(x − x²)dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = 1/2 − 1/3 = **1/6**. **Sanity:** the region sits inside the unit square (area 1) and is a slender sliver — 1/6 is plausible. **Deep point:** the order test at one interior point settles the whole strip (the order cannot change without a crossing, and there is none inside [0, 1]) — one sample point is a proof, not a guess.

**NEB-style (6m): Find the area between y = 4 − x² and y = x + 2.** — **Intersections:** 4 − x² = x + 2 ⟹ x² + x − 2 = 0 ⟹ (x + 2)(x − 1) = 0 ⟹ x = −2, 1. **Order test:** at x = 0: parabola 4 > line 2 ⟹ parabola on top throughout (no interior crossing). **Evaluate:** ∫₋₂¹[(4 − x²) − (x + 2)]dx = ∫₋₂¹(2 − x − x²)dx = [2x − x²/2 − x³/3]₋₂¹ = (2 − 1/2 − 1/3) − (−4 − 2 + 8/3) = (7/6) − (−10/3) = 7/6 + 20/6 = **27/6 = 9/2**. **Deep point:** the intersection solutions came from a quadratic whose factorisation was checked by expansion — the limits are the roots, and the order test confirmed a single-strip region; two integrals would have been wrong here, one was right.

**NEB-style (6m): Find the area of the region bounded by x = y² and x = 4.** — **Set-up choice:** the boundaries are x = y² (left) and x = 4 (right) — functions of y ⟹ **horizontal slices (dy)**. **Intersections:** y² = 4 ⟹ y = ±2 ⟹ limits y ∈ [−2, 2]. **Order:** at y = 1: right boundary 4 > left boundary y² = 1 ✓. **Evaluate:** ∫₋₂²(4 − y²)dy = 2∫₀²(4 − y²)dy (even) = 2[4y − y³/3]₀² = 2(8 − 8/3) = 2·(16/3) = **32/3**. **Cost comparison:** in dx this region needs two integrals (left boundary is √x for y > 0 and −√x for y < 0); in dy, one — the axis choice halved the work. **Deep point:** the slicing axis is decided by the boundary functions' form, and the symmetry doubling (even integrand in y) stacked a second saving; two cheap decisions replaced two hard integrals.

**NEB-style (6m): Find the area enclosed between y² = 2x and y = x − 4 — carefully identifying all boundary pieces.** — **Intersections:** substitute x = y + 4 into y² = 2x: y² = 2y + 8 ⟹ y² − 2y − 8 = 0 ⟹ (y − 4)(y + 2) = 0 ⟹ y = 4, −2 ⟹ points (8, 4) and (2, −2). **Slicing choice:** the parabola is naturally x = y²/2 (left boundary), the line x = y + 4 (right boundary) ⟹ **dy slices**, one integral. **Order test:** at y = 0: line x = 4 > parabola x = 0 ✓. **Evaluate:** ∫₋₂⁴[(y + 4) − y²/2]dy = [y²/2 + 4y − y³/6]₋₂⁴ = (8 + 16 − 64/6) − (2 − 8 + 8/6) = (24 − 32/3) − (−6 + 4/3) = 40/3 + 14/3 = **54/3 = 18**. **Deep point:** the classic trap is integrating in dx and missing that the region's left boundary changes at the vertex — the dy choice kept one formula per boundary; when curves are given as x = g(y), the horizontal slice is the honest native habitat.
keyPoints: Area between curves = integral of (top - bottom) dx, nonnegative; intersections from f = g supply the limits and any splits. Interior crossings swap top/bottom - partition and test one point per strip. The formula is |f - g| with the absolute value resolved by the order analysis. Choose the slicing axis that minimises splits (dy for x = g(y) boundaries). Verify symmetry before doubling a half.
summary: Area between two curves is |f − g| made structured: the intersections supply the limits and split points, the strip test fixes who is on top, and top-minus-bottom integrates the resolved order. Interior crossings swap the roles and demand partitioning; the slicing axis is chosen by counting splits; and verified symmetry doubles a half. Solve f = g first, sketch to bound the answer, and let a negative result send you back to the order test.

numericals:
**1. [Idea: an integral with a shifted inner function where the bounds must transform]** Evaluate $\int_0^1 \dfrac{2x}{(x^2+1)^3}\,dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Let $u = x^2+1$, so $du = 2x\,dx$. The limits transform: $x=0 \Rightarrow u=1$, and $x=1 \Rightarrow u=2$.
ewline
ewlineThe integral becomes$
ewline\int_1^2 u^{-3}du = \left[ rac{u^{-2}}{-2}ight]_1^2 = - rac12\left[ rac{1}{u^2}ight]_1^2 = - rac12\left( rac14 - 1ight) =  rac{3}{8}$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac38$.
ewline
ewline**Trap:** keeping limits $0$ and $1$ while integrating with respect to $u$. That gives $\left[- rac{1}{2u^2}ight]_0^1$, which is undefined at $u=0$ — the tell-tale sign that the substitution was mishandled.

**2. [Idea: by parts where the LIATE rule chooses the log term as $u$]** Evaluate $\int x\ln x\,dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** By parts, $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$.$^{ ullet}$ **LIATE** orders: Logarithmic before Algebraic, so take $u=\ln x$ and $dv=x\,dx$. Then $du= rac{dx}{x}$ and $v= rac{x^2}{2}$.
ewline
ewline$
ewline\int x\ln x\,dx =  rac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int  rac{x^2}{2}\cdot rac{dx}{x} =  rac{x^2}{2}\ln x -  rac12\int x\,dx =  rac{x^2}{2}\ln x -  rac{x^2}{4} + C$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac{x^2}{2}\ln x -  rac{x^2}{4}+C$, for $x>0$.
ewline
ewline**What went wrong if $u$ is chosen wrongly:** taking $u=x$, $dv=\ln x\,dx$ needs $\int \ln x\,dx$ first, which is itself an integral by parts — the problem gets strictly harder. **Also note:** on $[0,1]$ this integral is a proper one and $\int_0^1 x\ln x\,dx$ converges even though $\ln 0$ is undefined, since $x\ln x 	o 0$.

**3. [Idea: repeated by parts that must be stopped at a vanishing term]** Evaluate $\int x^2 e^x\,dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:**$^{ ullet}$ 1st application, $u=x^2$, $dv=e^x dx$, $du=2x\,dx$, $v=e^x$:$
ewline I = x^2e^x - 2\int xe^x\,dx$.$^{ ullet}$ 2nd application to the remaining integral, $u=x$, $dv=e^x dx$:$
ewline\int xe^x dx = xe^x - e^x$.
ewline
ewlineSubstitute back:$^{
ewline}I = x^2e^x - 2(xe^x - e^x) = x^2e^x - 2xe^x + 2e^x = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C$.
ewline
ewline**Verify by differentiating:** $ rac{d}{dx}\left[e^x(x^2-2x+2)ight] = e^x(x^2-2x+2) + e^x(2x-2) = e^x\cdot x^2$. ✓
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $e^x(x^2-2x+2)+C$. **The stopping rule:** stop as soon as a term becomes $0$; had a fourth application been attempted it would be meaningless.

**4. [Idea: symmetry collapses the work before any integration happens]** Evaluate $\int_{-2}^{2}\left(x^3\cos x + \sqrt{4-x^2}ight)dx$.
ewline
ewline**Solution: split by parity first.**$^{ ullet}$ $x^3$ is ODD and $\cos x$ is EVEN, so $x^3\cos x$ is ODD. An odd function integrates to $0$ over $[-2,2]$:$
ewline\int_{-2}^2 x^3\cos x\,dx = 0$.$^{ ullet}$ $\sqrt{4-x^2}$ is EVEN, so by King's rule $\int_{-2}^{2}\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx = 2\int_0^2 \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx$.
ewline
ewlineThis remaining integral is the area of a quarter circle of radius 2:$
ewline\int_0^2\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx =  rac14 \pi(2)^2 = \pi$.
ewline
ewlineSo the total is $0 + 2\pi$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $2\pi$. **The idea:** the odd part was dispatched with no calculus at all. Attempting to integrate $x^3\cos x$ directly needs repeated by parts for nothing.

**5. [Idea: the bounds do not determine the top curve — solve the intersection first]** Find the area bounded by $y=x^2$ and $y=\sqrt{x}$ for $x \ge 0$.
ewline
ewline**Solution:** Find the intersections: $x^2 = \sqrt{x} \Rightarrow x^4 = x \Rightarrow x(x^3-1)=0$, so $x=0$ and $x=1$.
ewline
ewline**Determine which is on top.** At $x= rac12$: $y_1 = x^2 =  rac14$ and $y_2 = \sqrt{x} =  rac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707$. Since $\sqrt{x} > x^2$ there, $\sqrt{x}$ is the TOP curve.
ewline
ewline**Area:**$^{ ullet}$ $\displaystyle A = \int_0^1 \left(\sqrt{x} - x^2ight)dx = \left[ rac{2}{3}x^{3/2} -  rac{x^3}{3}ight]_0^1 =  rac23 -  rac13 =  rac13$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** $ rac13$ square units. **Trap:** integrating $x^2-\sqrt{x}$ and getting $- rac13$. The top-minus-bottom convention means a negative answer signals the curves were named backwards, not that the area is negative.

**6. [Idea: the region is split because the bounding curve changes]** Find the area enclosed by $y=2x+1$, $y=x^2+2$ and the $y$-axis.
ewline
ewline**Solution:**$^{ ullet}$ The two curves meet where $2x+1 = x^2+2$, i.e. $x^2-2x+1=0$, i.e. $(x-1)^2=0$, so they are **tangent at $x=1$**, meeting at $(1,3)$.
ewline
ewline$^{ ullet}$ At $x=0$ the line gives $1$ and the parabola $2$, so the LINE is on top for $0\le x \le 1$ (tangent means they only just touch at $x=1$).$^{ ullet}$ The $y$-axis closes the region at $x=0$.
ewline
ewline**Area:**$^{ ullet}$ $\displaystyle A = \int_0^1 \left[(2x+1)-(x^2+2)ight]dx = \int_0^1\left(-x^2+2x-1ight)dx = \left[- rac{x^3}{3}+x^2-xight]_0^1 = - rac13+1-1 = - rac13$.
ewline
ewline**Answer:** area $=  rac13$ square units (the negative integral confirms the curves were named the wrong way round, so the true area is $ rac13$). **Note:** tangency gives a single intersection, so only one integral is needed — but the sign check is what catches the reversal.

subtopics.name: The formula
points: Area = integral from a to b of (upper curve - lower curve) dx
a and b are the x-coordinates of the intersection points
Subtracting handles the case where both curves are below the axis

subtopics.name: Finding the limits
points: Set the two equations equal and solve for x
Intersection points give the integration limits
If curves cross inside the interval, split the integral there

subtopics.name: Which curve is upper
points: Test a point between the intersections
The larger y-value at that test point belongs to the upper curve
Getting this backwards gives a negative area

subtopics.name: Choosing the variable
points: If the region is bounded left and right by curves, integrate with respect to y
Right minus left when integrating dy
Picking the wrong variable can force an unnecessary split

subtopics.name: Common exam shapes
points: Line and parabola, circle and line, two parabolas
Always sketch — the sketch is worth marks on its own
